summary: This informational memo from Toshiba describes the Flow Attribute Notification Protocol, used between neighbor nodes to manage cut-through packet forwarding. It documents a vendor protocol rather than a standard.

eli5.summary: Neighbors tell each other which packages can take the express lane.

questions: how do routers negotiate dedicated circuits with fanp
what happens if a router fails in fanp
subtitle: A neighbor-to-neighbor protocol for bypass-forwarding specific packet flows.

tldr.problem: Connection-oriented networks like ATM can forward cells at datalink speed without IP processing, but routers need to map IP packet flows to datalink connections. This mapping must be negotiated and maintained between neighbors.
tldr.mechanism: FANP lets routers discover when a long-lived flow (like HTTP) arrives, set up a dedicated virtual circuit (Dedicated-VC) to a neighbor, map the flow's source and destination IP addresses to that circuit, and refresh the mapping periodically. The protocol handles soft-state cleanup if a router fails.
tldr.outcome: Packets in recognized flows bypass IP processing and travel at datalink speed through cut-through paths, improving throughput for bulk data transfers. This vendor protocol competed with MPLS and other tunneling approaches.

today: RFC 2129 is an Informational RFC from Toshiba published in April 1997. It has not been obsoleted. The approach of cut-through forwarding for specific flows was superseded by MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) and later by modern SDN and OpenFlow, which provide more general and standardized flow-based forwarding.

sections.title: The Cut-Through Problem
sections.content:
Routers traditionally analyze every IP packet header to decide where to forward it. But connection-oriented datalinks like ATM and Frame Relay carry data in circuits identified by a Virtual Circuit ID (VCI) or other datalink-level label. If a router receives packets in a VCI and knows that all those packets belong to the same IP flow (same source and destination IP), it can forward the entire VCI at datalink speed without opening and parsing each IP header. This is cut-through packet forwarding.

The challenge is setting up the mapping between an IP flow and a datalink circuit, and keeping it fresh as router state changes. FANP solves this by letting neighbor routers (connected via ATM) notify each other of new flows and maintain the mapping over time.
sections.eli5: Normally a router reads every package's label. But if the router already knows 'packets in this express lane are all going to the same place,' it can skip reading and just route by the lane ID.

sections.title: Key Concepts
sections.content:
Dedicated-VC: A virtual circuit reserved for a specific IP flow. Unlike the Default-VC (used for normal hop-by-hop IP processing), a Dedicated-VC carries only packets belonging to one flow and can be forwarded without IP processing.

Flow ID: Identifies an IP packet flow. Currently defined as source IP address and destination IP address (note: not the same as IPv6 Flow ID).

VCID (Virtual Circuit ID): A datalink-independent identifier for a Dedicated-VC, constructed from the source node's ESI (End System Identifier) and a unique local identifier. This allows mapping even when VPI/VCI values differ at each hop.

Cut-through trigger: An arriving packet (typically to a port used by long-lived services like HTTP, FTP, or NNTP) that prompts a router to establish a Dedicated-VC for that flow.

Soft-state management: Dedicated-VCs and their mappings are temporary. If no packets arrive for a threshold period, the router automatically cleans up without explicit deletion messages, allowing recovery from router failures.
sections.eli5: A VCID is like a ticket number for an express lane. When a long transfer starts (like a movie download), the router recognizes it as a trigger and opens that lane between itself and the next router.

sections.title: The Five Procedures
sections.content:
FANP defines five procedures:

(1) Dedicated-VC Selection: Either pick an unused VC from a pre-provisioned pool, or request a new VC via ATM signaling. The VC is used as a unidirectional path from upstream to downstream.

(2) VCID Negotiation: The upstream node sends a PROPOSE message through the Dedicated-VC with the VCID and target IP address. The downstream node checks if the target matches its address, if policy allows, and if the VCID type is known. It then registers the mapping and responds with PROPOSE ACK through the Default-VC. If it declines, it sends an ERROR message. The upstream node retransmits PROPOSE up to five times before giving up.

(3) Flow-ID Notification: The upstream node sends an OFFER message through the Default-VC, containing the VCID, the flow ID (source and destination IP), and a refresh interval (recommended 120 seconds). The downstream node registers the mapping and replies with READY. If the downstream node cannot honor the refresh interval, it sends an ERROR.

(4) Flow-ID Refresh: As long as packets arrive on the Dedicated-VC, the downstream node periodically sends READY messages (at the negotiated interval). The upstream node can detect flow death and clean up when READY messages stop for a dead interval (recommended 6 minutes = 3x refresh). The downstream node removes the mapping after a removal period (recommended 20 minutes = 10x refresh) with no incoming packets.

(5) Flow-ID Removal: Either node can initiate. For PVC/VP circuits, they exchange REMOVE and REMOVE ACK messages. For SVC, they can either remove the mapping without releasing the VC, or tear down the VC via ATM signaling.
sections.eli5: Step 1: Set up the lane. Step 2: Shake hands on which lane (VCID). Step 3: Say what flow this lane is for. Step 4: Keep saying 'still here' while traffic flows. Step 5: Close the lane when traffic stops.

sections.title: Message Types and Formats
sections.content:
FANP defines seven message types:

PROPOSE (Op Code 0x10): Uses extended ATM-ARP format. Contains VCID type and VCID field; sent through the Dedicated-VC.

PROPOSE ACK (Op Code 1): Version (currently 1), VCID type, Flow-ID type, VCID. Checksum is 16-bit IP header checksum. Sent through Default-VC.

OFFER (Op Code 2): Carries VCID, Flow-ID, and Refresh Interval. Sent through Default-VC.

READY (Op Code 3): Confirms OFFER acceptance and is sent periodically as a heartbeat. Contains VCID and Flow-ID.

ERROR (Op Code 4): Sent when negotiation fails. Error codes include: unknown VCID type (1), unknown Flow-ID type (2), unknown VCID (3), resource unavailable (4), unsupported refresh interval (5), refused by policy (6). The message echoes back the VCID and Flow-ID from the rejected message.

REMOVE (Op Code 5): Initiates removal of a flow mapping. Contains VCID and optionally Flow-ID.

REMOVE ACK (Op Code 6): Acknowledges removal. Contains VCID.

All messages except PROPOSE are encapsulated in IP packets with Protocol ID 110.
sections.eli5: These seven message types are like saying 'I want to set up a lane' (PROPOSE), 'OK I accept' (PROPOSE ACK), 'here's what flow uses it' (OFFER), 'yep still active' (READY), 'no I can't' (ERROR), and 'shut it down' (REMOVE/REMOVE ACK).

sections.title: Robustness and Future Work
sections.content:
FANP is designed to operate correctly even if virtual circuits fail, control messages are lost, or a node goes down without notice. Soft-state timers handle node failures: if an upstream node dies, the downstream node stops receiving packets and automatically removes the mapping after the removal period. If a downstream node fails, the upstream node stops receiving READY messages and cleans up after the dead interval.

The protocol's scope is currently limited to flows defined by source and destination IP. The RFC identifies future enhancements: aggregated flows (combining multiple end-to-end flows into one VC to save resources), multicast, integration with RSVP for QoS, and IPv6 support. The RFC states that security issues are not discussed in the memo.
sections.eli5: The routers are tough: if a neighbor disappears, it figures out something is wrong and cleans up automatically. And the protocol can be extended later to handle more complex traffic and newer protocols.
